lesson_title: One Chicken Leg, One Million Bacteria
hook_text: Leave a chicken leg on a warm counter at lunchtime. By supper one bacterium on it can have become more than a million.
clip_script: One bacterium lands on a chicken leg on a warm kitchen counter. Bacteria multiply by splitting in two, and in warm, damp food some split every twenty minutes. After one hour, 8. After two hours, 64. After three hours, 512. After twenty splits, under seven hours, more than a million, all from one cell. That is why the fridge exists. But bacteria are only one of four families of micro-organisms. Viruses are not even cells, just instructions in a protein coat that hijack your cells to copy themselves. Bacteria are single cells with no nucleus: balls, rods and spirals. Protists are single cells with a nucleus, like the amoeba and the Plasmodium that causes malaria. Fungi are threads and budding cells, like bread mould and yeast. Here is why the family matters: antibiotics break bacterial walls, so they cure TB, but a virus has no wall. Antibiotics do nothing for the flu.
visual_style: A whiteboard chicken leg with a single dot that doubles on screen into 2, 4, 8, then a counter racing to 1 048 576; then four simple house icons labelled virus, bacterium, protist, fungus.
mood: Gross-out curiosity turning into practical sense.
pacing: Fast doubling countdown, a quick tour of the four houses, a firm last line about antibiotics.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sort any microbe in three questions.
